newsitem.title: USA: Ukraine IMF standby could be in place end August. [CORRECTED 22:58 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Ukraine IMF standby could be in place end August. [CORRECTED 22:58 GMT]

text.p: An IMF standby loan to Ukraine could be in place by the end of next month after talks in Washington and a final round of discussions with the government in Kiev, an IMF official said on Tuesday.
Adalbert Knobl, IMF mission chief to Ukraine, told Reuters he did not expect major difficulties during the final review in Kiev, due to start next Monday.
"I've learned my lessons with Ukraine, but as far as one can be confident, I am quite confident," he said.

Knobl declined to speculate on the size of the standby but he said the one-year loan could be replaced by a three-year Extended Fund Facility (EFF) credit at any time during the year if a raft of conditions were fulfilled.
"This is a bridging operation because some of the measures expected for the EFF were not approved in parliament," he said.

Ukrainian Deputy Prime Minister Serhiy Tyhypko has already complained that the IMF was not yet ready to release a $2.5-3 billion EFF and he described the IMF decision to look at a one-year credit as a personal defeat.

Tyhypko has said the standby could be "half the size of the EFF" but other sources indicated it could be smaller -- perhaps half the amount Ukraine had expected to receive in the first year of the EFF programme.

It was not clear how often the IMF would monitor the release of funds from a standby programme. A previous standby deal was subject to review every two months, but was paid out in monthly instalments.
Tyhypko, a former banker, has played a key role in efforts to kickstart Ukraine's stop-go reform programme since he was appointed to the government in April.

His new boss is likely to be Valery Pustovoitenko, a close ally of President Leonid Kuchma who was nominated last week to replace Pavlo Lazarenko and who is expected to outline his policy goals on Wednesday.
Lazarenko had been widely criticised in the West for stalling on economic reform. He quit this month, reportedly on grounds of ill health.
"There is no disputing that Ukraine has had problems and still has problems, but at least they got rid of Lazarenko," a senior European monetary source said last week.
Knobl said the new government team seemed to be moving forward on reform. "Tyhypko certainly seems dynamic and the ministers of finance and economics have some credentials as reformers," he said.
Knobl said the IMF expected the Ukrainian economy to return to growth next year (corrects from "this year") after severe declines in the years following the collapse of the Soviet Union.

He expected a GDP output decline of three percent this year, followed by a rise of three percent next year. The fact that this year's harvest was expected to be better than a dismal one in 1996 would help limit the fall in output.
He said inflation was likely to fall to 12 percent in 1998 from around 15 percent this year and almost 40 percent in 1996.
Knobl said the IMF was broadly satisfied with Ukrainian monetary policy, including a trading band pegging the hryvnia currency in a range of 1.70-1.90 to the dollar.
But improvements were needed to the tax system, including eliminating tax privileges and amending enterprise tax, income tax, payroll tax and value added tax.
